nameStory: The spotted sandpiper gets its name from the distinctive round black spots that dot its white breast and belly during breeding season. These bold polka-dot markings make it one of the easiest sandpipers to identify when they're dressed up for summer romance!
description: The spotted sandpiper is a small, energetic shorebird about the size of a robin. During breeding season, it sports a white belly covered in bold black spots, while in winter it becomes a more subdued brown and white. This lively bird has a unique habit of constantly bobbing its tail up and down, earning it the nickname "teeter-tail" among birdwatchers. It's one of our most common and widespread sandpipers in New England.

idTips.label: Constant tail bobbing
idTips.description: Watch for the distinctive up-and-down bobbing motion of the rear end - it's almost constant, like a nervous habit that never stops

idTips.label: Summer spots
idTips.description: Bold black polka dots cover the white breast and belly from May through July, making identification unmistakable during breeding season

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies with distinctive shallow wingbeats close to the water's surface, wings held stiffly downward showing white wing stripes

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: Robin-sized with a compact body, slightly longer legs than most small sandpipers, and a straight, medium-length bill

idTips.label: Winter appearance
idTips.description: Plain brown back with clean white underparts (no spots), but the constant bobbing behavior remains the same year-round

idTips.label: Voice
idTips.description: Clear, high whistled 'peet-weet-weet-weet' call that carries well across water, often heard before the bird is seen

habitat: Look for spotted sandpipers along almost any water's edge in New England - from rocky ocean shores and sandy beaches to muddy pond margins, stream banks, and even temporary puddles. They prefer areas where water meets land with some exposed mud, rocks, or vegetation for foraging. Unlike many sandpipers, they're equally at home in freshwater and saltwater environments, from mountain ponds to coastal marshes.

seasonality.spring: Arrive in April and May, with breeding plumage spots becoming more prominent. Listen for territorial 'peet-weet' calls along waterways.
seasonality.summer: Peak breeding season with full spotted plumage. Most active and vocal, often seen performing courtship flights over water.
seasonality.fall: Spots begin fading by late July. Young birds and adults in transitional plumage can be seen through September.
seasonality.winter: Most migrate south, but occasional birds may overwinter along ice-free coastal areas in plain brown and white plumage.

funFact: Spotted sandpipers have completely reversed gender roles - the females are larger, more colorful, and more aggressive, while the smaller, duller males do all the nest-sitting and chick care, sometimes tending multiple broods from different females at once!
confusionNotes: In winter plumage, spotted sandpipers can be confused with other small sandpipers, but remember the constant bobbing behavior - no other sandpiper bobs its tail as persistently. Think 'if it's bobbing, it's spotted' as your memory trick.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'sandpiper,' this species is equally comfortable away from sandy areas and is one of the few sandpipers that regularly nests far inland. The name 'sandpiper' originally referred to the piping calls these birds make rather than their habitat preferences.
compareHints: The spotted sandpiper is the only member of its genus regularly found in New England, making it unique among our sandpipers for its constant bobbing behavior. While other small sandpipers like least sandpipers may occasionally bob, none do it as continuously or dramatically as the spotted sandpiper's signature tail-pumping motion.
